extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy interested in free will, liberty, and moral psychology
extracted.subtask_description: Close-expository analysis of the concepts of liberty, volition, will, and desire as they relate to human agency; explains definitions, distinctions, and the psychological determinants of choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary opposed to involuntary
rubrics_metrics.description: Voluntary actions are those that depend on the agent's choice; involuntary actions are those the agent has no power to stop or start.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: an involuntary heartbeat or convulsive motions (chorea) cannot be stopped by thought and thus are not free; paralysis or the stocks hinder motion and remove freedom. Sitting still by preference is voluntary even for a paralytic. Voluntary is opposed to involuntary, not to necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty, what
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberty exists where the agent has power to take up or lay by thoughts or actions according to the preference of the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A waking person cannot be free to 'not think' but can remove attention from one idea to another; some ideas (e.g., pain on the rack or a boisterous passion) may be unavoidable and so remove liberty until the mind regains power to stop or continue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary agents vs. agents with volition
rubrics_metrics.description: Where thought is wholly wanting or where the power to act/forbear according to thought is absent, necessity rules and the agent is a necessary agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an agent capable of volition is forced to begin or continue an action contrary to preference, this is compulsion; if hindered from stopping an action contrary to volition, this is restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misplaced question: 'Is the will free?'
rubrics_metrics.description: The author argues the question 'whether the will is free' is improper because liberty is a power belonging to agents, not an attribute of the will itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: asking whether the will is free is as absurd as asking whether sleep is swift or virtue square — these predicates don't apply to those subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volition (definition and warning about language)
rubrics_metrics.description: Volition is the mind's act of knowingly exerting dominion over the person by employing or withholding parts of the person in action; will is the faculty enabling that power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terms like ordering, choosing, preferring are used but may not perfectly express volition; volition is the mind's determination to produce, continue, or stop any action insofar as it depends on us.

rubrics_metrics.name: Powers belonging to Agents
rubrics_metrics.description: Will is one power or ability, freedom another; powers properly belong to agents (substances), not to powers themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To ask whether one power (will) has another power (freedom) is absurd. Freedom is attributed to things that can act — to agents — not to powers in isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: How the will is improperly treated as an agent
rubrics_metrics.description: Calling the will a faculty who 'acts' leads to conceptual confusion and invites personification of faculties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If faculties are spoken of as distinct beings that act, one would need speaking, walking, dancing faculties, etc. This misleads by making abilities into agents.

rubrics_metrics.name: This way of talking causes confusion of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating mental faculties as agents produces confusion because one power does not operate on another; the mind (agent) exerts multiple powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: the power of thinking does not operate on the power of choosing any more than dancing operates on singing; it is the agent that exerts both powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Powers are relations, not agents
rubrics_metrics.description: Powers (abilities) are relational properties of the agent; they do not themselves act — the agent acts by exercising powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actual thoughts may occasion volition and vice versa, but it is the agent (the mind) that operates. Freedom or lack of it attaches to the agent, not to the power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty belongs not to the Will
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributing freedom to 'faculties' (like the will) rather than to the agent has caused philosophical confusion; faculties are names for powers but are not independent agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical practice of invoking faculties (digestive, expulsive, motive) obscures that something able to digest is what acts; similarly, the will as a faculty shouldn't be treated as an acting agent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty attributed to the Agent, not the will
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper question is whether a man (the agent) is free, i.e., whether he can, by choice, make actions exist or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If by thought one can move a finger or produce speech, one is free in respect of that action; liberty consists in the power to act or forbear acting according to one's determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: A man is not free in respect of willing
rubrics_metrics.description: While a man may be free to perform or forbear actions, he is not free in the act of willing itself once an action is proposed to thought — willing must occur one way or another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mind cannot avoid some determination when an action is proposed; the act of volition (willing) is necessarily one of the options, so the agent lacks liberty with respect to willing itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty is freedom to execute what is willed
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom consists in the power to execute or forbear the actions one wills; being able to do or not do an action is the mark of liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a man sitting is free to walk because he can stand up and walk; a man falling down a precipice is not free because he cannot stop the motion even if he wills it.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Will determined by something without it (what moves the will?)
rubrics_metrics.description: The question of 'what determines the will' should be answered: the mind determines it; more specifically, present satisfaction or, for change, present uneasiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motive for continuing is present satisfaction; motive for change is uneasiness. The author will elaborate uneasiness as the key determining factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Will and Desire must not be confounded
rubrics_metrics.description: Will (volition) is distinct from desire; will concerns actions the agent directs, whereas desire is an uneasiness for some absent good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: one may will an action while desiring the opposite outcome; desire and will can run counter. Will attends to actions in the agent's power; desire is an affective state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uneasiness determines the Will
rubrics_metrics.description: The immediate determinant of volition in most instances is present uneasiness (desire as an uneasiness for an absent good), not contemplation of the greater good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Desire as uneasiness motivates action to remove the pain; examples include physical pains and appetites engineered to preserve life and species (hunger, thirst).

rubrics_metrics.name: Desire is Uneasiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Desire is characterized as a state of uneasiness for want of an absent good; strong desire can be felt as sickness in the heart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intensity of desire correlates with intensity of uneasiness; life becomes burdensome under persistent unremoved desire.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Uneasiness of Desire determines the Will
rubrics_metrics.description: Good and evil (present/absent) influence the mind, but immediate volitional determination arises from the uneasiness of desire fixed on an absent good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes positive absent goods (desire for good things) and relief desires (ease from pain); both manifest as uneasiness that drives will to act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uneasiness is the spring of action
rubrics_metrics.description: When a person is without uneasiness (content), there is little motivation to act; natural pains and desires are built to produce necessary action for preservation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If mere contemplation of good were enough to motivate, natural pains like hunger would be unnecessary; example invoked: 'It is better to marry than to burn' — a burning desire pushes action more than distant good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greatest positive good does not by itself determine the Will
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledging a greater good does not determine will unless desire (uneasiness) for it is present; present uneasiness can override contemplation of greater goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a person content in poverty won't act to obtain riches despite acknowledging their value; a drunkard may acknowledge health's superiority but is driven by habitual uneasiness to drink.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of uneasiness is first step to happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Agents aim at happiness; as long as uneasiness exists, the immediate aim is to remove it, which explains why uneasiness determines choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pain spoils enjoyment; thus action is driven first to remove pain/uneasiness as that is necessary to regain happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Because Uneasiness alone is present
rubrics_metrics.description: Uneasiness determines will partly because it is immediately present while absent goods are not; absent goods only determine the will when they raise desire and associated uneasiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ideas of absent goods remain speculative until desire makes them present by uneasiness; e.g., contemplation of heaven does not necessarily move the will absent felt desire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Because all who allow the Joys of Heaven possible, pursue them not
rubrics_metrics.description: If the will were determined merely by the greater good in view, people would consistently pursue the greatest good (e.g., heaven); yet experience shows they often do not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hence absent greater goods fail to fix the will unless accompanied by present uneasiness that raises desire to act.

rubrics_metrics.name: But any great Uneasiness is never neglected
rubrics_metrics.description: A very great prevailing uneasiness, once it seizes the mind, keeps the will steadily directed until it is removed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: vehement bodily pain, ungovernable passion, or impatient desire for revenge will monopolize the will and understanding as long as the uneasiness persists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desire accompanies all Uneasiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Most passions involve uneasiness plus desire; desire is normally present with aversion, fear, anger, envy, shame, etc., and thereby influences the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even joy involves desire (fear of losing it, desire to continue). The present strongest uneasiness will shift the will to new actions when it arises.

rubrics_metrics.name: The most pressing Uneasiness naturally determines the Will
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple uneasinesses coexist, ordinarily the most pressing one (judged capable of being then removed) has precedence in determining the next action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agents are distracted by different desires; practical choice is typically governed by which uneasiness is most exigent and removable in the situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volition and action: inclusive definition of 'action'
rubrics_metrics.description: For brevity, 'action' includes the forbearance of any proposed action (sitting still or holding peace) because these forbearances require determination of the will as much as actions do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This semantic choice avoids confusion when discussing will: 'action' can mean doing or refraining, both requiring volitional determination.
